title: Two Promised Sons: John and Jesus Announced
summary: Luke opens with a formal preface explaining that he has investigated everything carefully to write an orderly account for Theophilus. In the temple the angel Gabriel tells the aged priest Zechariah that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way for the Lord; Zechariah doubts and is struck mute. Six months later Gabriel tells Mary, a virgin in Nazareth, that she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear Jesus, the Son of God and heir of David's throne. Mary visits Elizabeth and sings of God's mercy, John is born and named, and Zechariah, his speech restored, prophesies God's salvation.
story:
The Old Testament closed with a promise that God would send his messenger, Elijah, before the day of the Lord (Malachi 3:1, 4:5-6), and in the traditional reckoning of both Jews and Christians no new prophetic voice arose for about four centuries after it. Luke begins the story again in the temple, among faithful Jews who have been waiting, and he tells it in language that sounds like the Old Testament on purpose. Zechariah and Elizabeth are Abraham and Sarah again, the angel is Daniel's Gabriel, and Mary's song echoes Hannah's.

The chapter sets up the whole Gospel. Two births are announced, two sons with distinct roles: John the forerunner, great before the Lord, and Jesus the Lord himself, great without qualification. Behind both stands a God who is keeping the promises he made to Abraham (verses 55 and 73) and to David (verses 32 and 69). The chapter moves from a priest at the center of Israel's worship to a young woman in a village no Scripture had ever named, and from doubt struck silent to faith that sings. Everything that follows in Luke and Acts flows from what God begins here: the Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah will fill Jesus at the Jordan (3:22) and the church at Pentecost (Acts 2:4), and the humble whom Mary sees lifted up will be the poor to whom Jesus preaches good news (4:18).
historical:
Herod, called king of Judea in verse 5, is Herod the Great, whom the Roman Senate named king in 40 BC and who took Jerusalem in 37 BC and ruled until his death, usually dated to 4 BC (a minority of scholars argue for 1 BC). He was a gifted and ruthless client king, a great builder who began rebuilding the Jerusalem temple on a lavish scale in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and a man feared even by his own family; he executed his wife Mariamne and three of his sons. The events of this chapter take place in the last years of his reign, and Matthew 2 agrees that Jesus was born while he lived.

The temple was served by priests descended from Aaron, divided into twenty-four courses that took turns serving for a week at a time, about twice a year, with all courses present at the great festivals. The course of Abijah was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10) and was still active after the exile (Nehemiah 12:17). Josephus, himself from a priestly family of the first course (Life 2), says the priests were so numerous that each division numbered over five thousand men (Against Apion 2.108), and lists of the courses survive among the Dead Sea Scrolls (the Mishmarot texts, 4Q320-330). With so many priests, duties were assigned by lot. The Mishnah describes the lots cast each morning for the tasks of the daily offering, with a separate lot for the incense among those who had never offered it (m. Tamid 5:2), and the Babylonian Talmud says no priest offered the incense twice (b. Yoma 26a). Incense was burned on the golden altar in the holy place morning and evening (Exodus 30:7-8), while worshipers prayed in the courts outside; afterward the priests pronounced the blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 over the people (m. Tamid 7:2), the blessing Zechariah could not give. His moment in the sanctuary was likely the high point of his priestly life.

The second scene is set in Nazareth, a small farming village in the hills of lower Galilee. It is named nowhere in the Old Testament, in Josephus, or in the Mishnah and Talmud. Excavations show a village of simple houses cut partly into the rock, with cisterns, storage pits, and agricultural terraces, and its earliest mention outside Christian writings is a synagogue inscription of the priestly courses from Caesarea, dated to the third or fourth century AD. The contrast Luke draws is pointed: one announcement comes in the holy place of the greatest building in Judea, the other in a village from which no one expected anything (John 1:46). An Aramaic fragment from Qumran, 4Q246, speaks of a figure who will be called son of God and son of the Most High and whose kingdom is everlasting; whether he is a Messiah or a hostile king claiming divine titles is debated, but the text shows that Gabriel's titles in verses 32 and 35 were already current in Judea.
cultural:
Barrenness in the ancient world was a deep grief and often a public shame, which is why Elizabeth speaks of God taking away her disgrace among the people (verse 25). It was usually blamed on the woman; verse 7 gives the cause in Elizabeth alone, as any ancient reader would expect. A childless couple had no one to carry the family name or care for them in age, and many assumed that God had withheld children for a reason. Luke refuses that inference by calling both of them righteous and blameless first (verse 6). The Old Testament tells several stories of barren women whom God opened to bear children of destiny: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother, and Hannah. Luke's readers who knew their Scriptures would recognize the pattern at once, and Elizabeth's words echo Rachel's at Joseph's birth (Genesis 30:23). John's abstention from wine and strong drink resembles the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, and like Samson and Samuel he is set apart from birth.

Marriage in first-century Judaism took place in two stages. Betrothal was a binding legal agreement, often made when a girl was in her early or middle teens, after which the couple were called husband and wife and could be separated only by divorce (Deuteronomy 22:23-24 already treats a betrothed woman's unfaithfulness as adultery). Some time later, commonly up to a year for a young bride (m. Ketubot 5:2), the bride moved into her husband's home and the marriage was completed. Mary was betrothed to Joseph but still living in her own family's house (verse 56). A pregnancy in that interval would expose her to suspicion, which is the situation Matthew 1:18-25 describes from Joseph's side.

Naming a son on the day of his circumcision, the eighth day as commanded in Genesis 17:12 and Leviticus 12:3, appears here and in 2:21 among the earliest clear witnesses to the custom. Sons were usually named after a father or grandfather, which is why the relatives object to the name John; the high-priestly families repeated names across generations, and Tobit names his son Tobias (Tobit 1:9). Zechariah writes on a pinakidion, a small writing tablet usually made of wood coated with wax and written on with a stylus, the everyday notepad of the Roman world. The hill country of Judah (verse 39) was the upland region around Jerusalem, where many priestly families lived when not on duty; from about the sixth century Christians identified Zechariah's town with Ein Karem, west of Jerusalem, though the Gospel gives no name. The trip from Nazareth to the Judean hills was roughly eighty miles, several days on foot, which gives weight to Luke's note that Mary went in haste.
literary:
Luke's preface (verses 1 to 4) is a single long sentence in polished literary Greek, balanced in two halves: what others have done (verses 1 and 2) and what the author does (verses 3 and 4). It names predecessors, sources, method, addressee, and purpose, as Greek historians did (Thucydides 1.22, Polybius 12.27-28), and Loveday Alexander (1993) showed that its closest formal parallels are the plainer prefaces of Greek technical and scientific treatises. Then, from verse 5, the Greek changes and sounds like the Septuagint, with Hebrew-style openings (‘it happened in the days of Herod’), chains of clauses joined by and, and phrases from Genesis, Judges, and Samuel, as if the story itself required the language of Scripture.

The chapter is built as a diptych, two panels set side by side. Each announcement has the same parts: the appearance of Gabriel, fear, ‘Do not be afraid’, the promise of a son and his name, a description of his greatness, a question, and a sign. The parallels make the differences stand out. Zechariah is a priest in the temple; Mary is a young woman in a village. Zechariah asks for proof and is silenced; Mary asks how and consents. John will be great before the Lord; Jesus will be great, Son of the Most High, with a kingdom that never ends. John will be filled with the Spirit; Jesus will be conceived by the Spirit. The two strands meet in the Visitation (verses 39 to 56), where the unborn John leaps before the unborn Jesus, and then separate again for the birth of John (verses 57 to 80), whose matching birth of Jesus follows in chapter 2. Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) laid out this step parallelism in detail; René Laurentin (1957) read the whole of chapters 1 and 2 as a close meditation on Daniel 9 and Malachi 3.

The chapter includes two of the church's oldest hymns, Mary's song (verses 46 to 55, called the Magnificat from its first word in Latin) and Zechariah's (verses 68 to 79, called the Benedictus). Both are woven almost entirely from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1-10), the Psalms, and Isaiah. Whether Luke wrote them or took them over from early Jewish Christian circles is debated: Brown and Stephen Farris (The Hymns of Luke's Infancy Narratives, 1985) argued that they come from such circles, perhaps first composed in Hebrew, while others think Luke composed them himself in the Septuagint's idiom. Either way they interpret the narrative: the songs tell the reader what the births mean.

outline.t: Gabriel announces John's birth to Zechariah
Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary
The birth and naming of John

doctrines.note: The Holy Spirit comes upon Mary and the power of the Most High overshadows her, so that the holy one born of her is called the Son of God (verse 35). The conception is God's creative act, without a human father and without any hint of a divine partner, and Elizabeth already calls the unborn child “my Lord” (verse 43). The church confesses on this chapter's witness that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, and the Council of Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, to affirm that the one she bore is one person, truly God.

Gabriel's words gather Israel's royal hopes onto Jesus: he will be called Son of the Most High, receive the throne of his father David, and reign over the house of Jacob with a kingdom that will never end, the promise first made to David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16. Zechariah, a priest of Aaron's line, praises God first not for his own son but for the horn of salvation raised in David's house (verse 69).

Mary and Zechariah both interpret these births as God remembering his covenant, the oath he swore to Abraham (verses 55 and 72-73), and his promises through the prophets. God's remembering is an act, not a mental event. What happens here is not a new idea but God keeping his word, which Gabriel sums up in verse 37: “For no word from God will ever fail.”

Zechariah, a righteous priest, asks for proof and is silenced; Mary, a young woman in a village, asks how and then surrenders: “I am the Lord’s servant.” Elizabeth names the difference: “Blessed is she who has believed.” Faith here is trust in God's word before its fulfillment is seen, and it thinks and questions without demanding a sign.

Mary's song makes God's rescue of the humble and the hungry part of Israel's salvation, not an addition to it: he looks on the humble state of his servant, brings down rulers, exalts the lowly, fills the hungry, and sends the rich away empty (verses 48-53). Poverty is not presented as a virtue but as the place where God's mercy arrives, a theme Luke carries into the Beatitudes and woes (6:20-26).

words.note: Diēgēsis, a narrative or account. It occurs only here in the New Testament, though it was the ordinary Greek word for a historical narrative (2 Maccabees 2:32 uses it of that book's own account). Luke uses it of the ‘many’ accounts before his, including his own. The word claims a connected story of events, not a collection of sayings or a book of proofs.

Asphaleia, security, safety, certainty. It occurs three times in the New Testament: here, of a prison ‘securely locked’ (Acts 5:23), and of the false ‘peace and security’ of 1 Thessalonians 5:3. BDAG gives both a physical sense (safety) and a mental one (certainty, the reliability of a report). It stands last in the preface for emphasis: the aim of Luke's whole work is that Theophilus may know that what he was taught stands on firm ground.

Charitoō, to favor or bestow grace. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in Ephesians 1:6, where God has freely given grace to believers in the Beloved. Gabriel greets Mary with its perfect passive participle, one who has been favored, used almost as a name. The emphasis falls on God's free choice, which verse 30 restates plainly (you have found favor with God). The Latin gratia plena, full of grace, behind the Ave Maria, has been read by Catholic interpreters as a lasting state of grace and by Protestant interpreters as grace received rather than given; the verb itself says she is the object of God's favor.

Episkiazō, to overshadow, cast a shadow over. It occurs five times in the New Testament: here, three times of the cloud at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:5, Mark 9:7, Luke 9:34), and of Peter's shadow in Acts 5:15. In the Greek Old Testament it describes the cloud of God's glory settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). Gabriel's word presents the conception of Jesus as an act of God's creative presence, like the glory filling the tent, not a divine union of the kind found in pagan myths.

Tapeinōsis, lowliness, humble state, humiliation. It occurs four times in the New Testament (here, Acts 8:33 quoting Isaiah 53:8, Philippians 3:21, and James 1:10). Mary sings that God has looked on the humble state of his servant, and Hannah used the same word in the Greek Old Testament when she prayed for a son (1 Samuel 1:11). The word can mean a lowly social position as well as an inner humility, and here both are in view: a young woman of no standing whom God regards.

Eleos, mercy. It occurs about twenty-seven times in the New Testament and five times in this chapter alone (verses 50, 54, 58, 72, 78). In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew hesed, God's steadfast covenant love, and that is its sense here: the mercy remembered is the loyal love God swore to Abraham. The word is the chapter's thread, running from Mary's song through the neighbors' rejoicing to the tender mercy of Zechariah's last lines.

Episkeptomai, to visit, look after, come to help. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament, three of them in Luke's Gospel (1:68, 1:78, 7:16). It translates the Hebrew paqad, the verb for God's coming to his people in the exodus (Exodus 4:31) and to Naomi's people with bread (Ruth 1:6). Zechariah's song opens and closes with it: God has visited his people, and the Dawn will visit from on high. When Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because it did not recognize the time of its visitation (19:44), Luke uses the related noun.

Anatolē, a rising, especially of the sun, hence the east and the dawn. It occurs about ten times in the New Testament, usually meaning the east (the magi come from the east, Matthew 2:1). Zechariah speaks of the Dawn that will visit us from on high. In the Greek Old Testament the same word translates the Hebrew tsemach, Branch, a title for the coming king from David's line (Jeremiah 23:5, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12), so both images may be in play: a sunrise and a royal shoot.

christ:
Luke 1 says more about who Jesus is before his birth than any other chapter in the Gospels. He is Jesus, a Greek form of Joshua, whose name means the Lord saves. He is the Son of the Most High and the Son of God, conceived by the Holy Spirit, so that his divine sonship is not something he later achieves but belongs to him from the beginning of his human life. He is the heir of David who will reign forever, fulfilling 2 Samuel 7:12-16, Psalm 89, and Isaiah 9:6-7, where a child on David's throne has a government without end. Elizabeth calls him “the mother of my Lord” while he is still unborn, using the word kurios that Luke's narrative uses in the same chapter for God himself, and John leaps for joy in his presence.

The chapter's Old Testament echoes also point to who he is. John is to go before ‘the Lord their God’ (verses 16 and 17) and prepare the way for the Lord (verse 76), the language Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 use of God's own coming; when the one who follows John turns out to be Jesus, the reader learns that in Jesus the Lord himself has come. Zechariah's song calls his coming a visit from God, the Dawn from on high shining on those in darkness and the shadow of death, echoing Isaiah 9:2, where the light rises on Galilee before a royal child is announced. Some readers see in the Visitation a further pattern: as the ark of the covenant stayed three months in the house of Obed-edom and brought blessing (2 Samuel 6:9-11), Mary, carrying the Lord, stays three months with Elizabeth (verse 56); René Laurentin pressed the parallel, while Raymond Brown and Joseph Fitzmyer thought it too loose to prove Luke's design.

The chapter also shows the character of his coming. He comes through a humble young woman in an obscure village, and the song his mother sings describes a God who scatters the proud and lifts the humble, the pattern his whole life will follow, from a manger to a cross to an empty tomb. Paul's words that God sent his Son, “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4), are told here as a story, and the church's confession that the eternal Son became man without ceasing to be God has this chapter as one of its foundations.
interpretation:
The church fathers read Luke 1 as the opening of the Gospel of the priesthood and of Mary. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8, around 180) gave Luke the calf among the four living creatures because it begins with Zechariah offering sacrifice, and Jerome kept that symbol. Irenaeus also set Mary's obedience against Eve's disobedience (Against Heresies 3.22.4), a theme Justin Martyr had begun (Dialogue with Trypho 100). Origen's homilies on Luke, preached at Caesarea and preserved in Jerome's Latin, give their first several sermons to this chapter, and Ambrose's Exposition of Luke (about 387) made the Annunciation and the Magnificat central to Latin reflection on Mary. Augustine (On Holy Virginity 4) read Mary's question in verse 34 as evidence that she had resolved to remain a virgin, a reading still common in Catholic interpretation. The Council of Ephesus (431) confirmed the title Theotokos, God-bearer, against Nestorius, with Elizabeth's ‘mother of my Lord’ among its texts. Bede preached on the Annunciation and the Visitation in his Homilies on the Gospels in eighth-century Northumbria.

Jewish tradition did not comment on Luke, but it answered its claims. The second-century pagan Celsus, as quoted by Origen (Against Celsus 1.28 and 1.32), repeated a story that Jesus was the son of a soldier named Panthera, and the Tosefta (t. Hullin 2:22-24) mentions healing in the name of Yeshua ben Pantera. Justin's Trypho already disputed the Christian use of Isaiah 7:14 (Dialogue 43 and 67), and the medieval Toledot Yeshu retold Jesus' birth as illegitimate. In modern scholarship Jewish and Christian readers have studied the chapter together, as Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III do in their joint commentary (2018), reading its priests, prayers, and hopes against the Jewish sources it echoes.

In the Middle Ages the chapter shaped daily prayer and devotion. Gabriel's and Elizabeth's greetings became the Ave Maria, the Angelus was prayed at morning, noon, and evening, the Magnificat was sung at Vespers and the Benedictus at Lauds, and the Feast of the Annunciation was kept on 25 March, nine months before Christmas. Painters made the Annunciation one of the great subjects of Western art: Fra Angelico's frescoes at San Marco in Florence (1440s), Leonardo da Vinci's Annunciation in the Uffizi (about 1472 to 1476), and many others show the angel, the book in Mary's hands, and the dove of the Spirit.

The Reformers kept the canticles and honored Mary while rejecting prayers to her. Martin Luther wrote a commentary on the Magnificat in 1521, dedicated to the young Prince John Frederick of Saxony, as a lesson in how God regards the lowly and the mighty; Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) commends Mary's faith as a pattern for all believers. The Book of Common Prayer (1549) kept the Benedictus at Morning Prayer and the Magnificat at Evening Prayer. Monteverdi's Vespers (1610) and Bach's Magnificat (first version for Christmas 1723 in Leipzig) are among its great settings. In an Advent sermon in London in 1933 Dietrich Bonhoeffer called the Magnificat a revolutionary song, and Latin American liberation theologians, Gustavo Gutiérrez among them, made it central to their reading of God's preference for the poor.

Modern critical study has concentrated on sources and structure: the step parallelism of John and Jesus, the origin of the canticles, and the relation of Luke's account to Matthew's. Raymond Brown's The Birth of the Messiah (1977; updated 1993) remains the standard treatment, and Laurentin's Structure et théologie de Luc I-II (1957) the chief case for dense Old Testament typology. In the Revised Common Lectionary the Annunciation (verses 26 to 38) is read on the fourth Sunday of Advent in Year B and the Visitation (verses 39 to 45, with the Magnificat) in Year C.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 28 the Byzantine manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add ‘blessed art thou among women’, borrowed from Elizabeth's greeting in verse 42; the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus among them) lack it there. In verse 35 the Byzantine text adds ‘of thee’, giving the KJV's ‘that holy thing which shall be born of thee’. In verse 37 the earliest manuscripts read ‘from God’, which suits the BSB's ‘no word from God will ever fail’, while the Byzantine text reads ‘with God’, which suits the KJV's ‘with God nothing shall be impossible’; the noun rhēma can mean either word or thing, as the Hebrew davar can.

In verse 46 every Greek manuscript reads ‘Mary said’, but three Old Latin manuscripts read ‘Elizabeth said’, and Niceta of Remesiana (about AD 400) attributes the song to Elizabeth. Alfred Loisy and Adolf von Harnack argued that Luke wrote only ‘she said’; nearly all scholars keep Mary. In verse 78 the earliest manuscripts read the future ‘will visit’, printed in the critical editions and the BSB, while the Byzantine text reads ‘has visited’, matching verse 68. In verse 50 the wording of ‘from generation to generation’ differs slightly without changing the sense. Translation rather than text explains the KJV's ‘most surely believed among us’ in verse 1, where most modern versions read ‘fulfilled’: the participle can mean either.

teach.big: God keeps his ancient promises by coming himself in the child Mary will bear, and he gives his word to the doubting and the humble alike, silencing unbelief and lifting up those who receive his word in faith.

outline.t: The Christian faith rests on events that happened and were witnessed, handed down, and carefully investigated, so that believers can know its certainty.
God hears long-delayed prayers in his own time; even a righteous priest can doubt, and God's discipline of doubt is also mercy.
God's favor falls on the unlikely, and the child promised is David's heir and God's Son, conceived by the Spirit; faith answers with honest questions and full surrender.
The Spirit's first work in the Gospel is to recognize Jesus, and the first beatitude blesses the one who believes God's word.
Mary's song teaches that God's mercy reverses the world's order, humbling the proud and lifting the lowly, in faithfulness to Abraham.
Obedience to God's word breaks Zechariah's silence, and his first words are praise.
God's salvation is a visit from on high that fulfills the promises to David and Abraham, brings forgiveness of sins, and guides his people into peace.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats Zechariah as a villain and Mary as a model of perfect certainty. Luke calls Zechariah righteous and blameless, and his doubt is the doubt of a faithful man worn down by decades of unanswered prayer; Mary is troubled and asks questions. The contrast is between demanding a sign and seeking understanding, not between bad and good people. The second reduces the Magnificat either to a political manifesto or to purely inner spirituality. The song speaks of real rulers, real hunger, and real riches, and also of the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; Luke keeps both, and so should the teacher.

The third is to turn the annunciation into a lesson on saying yes to God's plan for one's career or personal dreams. Mary's consent is to bear the Messiah, a unique vocation, and while her faith is a model, the chapter is first about what God does. The fourth is to read the preface as a claim that Luke was an eyewitness; he says the opposite, that he depended on eyewitnesses and investigated. Finally, avoid presenting Elizabeth's barrenness as a punishment later lifted, or pregnancy as the reward of righteousness; Luke explicitly separates the two.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on those who have prayed for children for years without an answer, and on those who have lost pregnancies. Teach it with care: Elizabeth's joy is real, but the chapter does not promise every faithful couple a child, and some in the room will hear it as an accusation. Luke's point that Elizabeth and Zechariah were righteous before they had a child can be a comfort: childlessness is not a sign of God's displeasure. The story of Zechariah also speaks gently to doubters, including those who once believed easily and now find it hard. His doubt did not stop God's promise, and his silence ended in praise. Mary's situation, a young woman facing scandal and misunderstanding, may speak to those carrying an unexpected or difficult pregnancy.

hard.q: Is the virginal conception of Jesus history or legend?
hard.a:
The objection is old and comes from several directions. The second-century critic Celsus, as quoted by Origen (Against Celsus 1.28 and 1.32), claimed that Mary had been put away for adultery with a soldier named Panthera and that the virgin story covered the scandal, and a similar name appears in rabbinic sources (t. Hullin 2:22-24). Jewish readers from Justin's Trypho onward (Dialogue with Trypho 43, 67) have pointed out that Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew speaks of an almah, a young woman, not necessarily a virgin, and that the sign was given to King Ahaz. Modern critics add that Mark, John, and Paul never mention a virginal conception, that the Greek and Roman world told stories of heroes and rulers with divine fathers, and that the infancy narratives are the most stylized parts of the Gospels. Gerd Lüdemann (Virgin Birth?, 1998) concluded that Jesus was conceived in the ordinary way, possibly outside marriage; Jane Schaberg (The Illegitimacy of Jesus, 1987) argued that Matthew and Luke inherited a tradition of illegitimate conception and wrote of God's vindication of Mary; and Andrew Lincoln, a Christian scholar (Born of a Virgin?, 2013), argued that the Gospel writers may not have meant a biological claim and that faith in the incarnation does not depend on it.

Those who hold the historic confession answer on several fronts. J. Gresham Machen (The Virgin Birth of Christ, 1930) and Raymond Brown (The Virginal Conception and Bodily Resurrection of Jesus, 1973, and The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) argued that Matthew and Luke tell the story independently, from Joseph's side and from Mary's, yet agree on the essentials: a betrothed virgin, conception by the Holy Spirit, and birth in David's line, which points to an older tradition behind both. Brown, a cautious Catholic critic, judged that the scientifically controllable evidence cannot settle the question but that the evidence leans more toward historicity than away from it. The silence of Mark, John, and Paul is not denial, since Mark begins with the adult Jesus, and some read John 1:13 and 8:41 as aware of controversy about his birth. The pagan parallels involve gods physically uniting with women, quite unlike Luke's reverent account of the Spirit's overshadowing, and Jewish Christians would hardly invent a story that exposed Mary to the charge Celsus made; the Panthera story itself, on this view, presupposes that Jesus' birth was known to be unusual. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 110 (To the Ephesians 19, To the Smyrnaeans 1), already treats the virgin birth as part of the church's confession. For historic Christianity, confessed in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, it belongs to the article of faith that Jesus is fully human, born of a woman, and the eternal Son whose life did not begin in Mary's womb but entered the world there. The Jewish objection on Isaiah 7:14 deserves an honest answer: Luke does not quote that verse, and Christians differ on how directly it predicted the event.

hard.q: Are Luke's first two chapters history, or a composition modeled on the Old Testament?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection notes how closely these chapters imitate Scripture. The Greek shifts suddenly into Septuagint style; the story of Zechariah and Elizabeth follows Abraham and Sarah and the birth of Samuel scene by scene; Gabriel comes from Daniel; the songs are mosaics of Old Testament phrases. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated such narratives as myth, the early church's way of clothing its faith in Jesus in the forms of Israel's stories, and many modern critics, including Geza Vermes (The Nativity, 2006) and Marcus Borg and John Dominic Crossan (The First Christmas, 2007), read the birth stories as theological overtures rather than reports. They point out that no one outside the family could have witnessed the annunciations, and that the canticles look like hymns Luke has placed in his characters' mouths.

Others answer that literary shaping and historical reference are not opposites. Luke's own preface claims careful investigation of eyewitness tradition, and his repeated notes that Mary treasured these things (2:19, 2:51) may point to the family as a source; Richard Bauckham (Gospel Women, 2002) has argued for the historical plausibility of Luke's named women. I. Howard Marshall and Darrell Bock, in their commentaries, hold that Luke used family traditions from Palestinian Jewish Christian circles, which would explain the Semitic style better than free invention by a Gentile author. Brown and Stephen Farris think the canticles came from such circles, which would make them early rather than late. The Old Testament patterns can be read as Luke's way of saying that God was acting as he had before, not as evidence that nothing happened. Scholars who share a high view of Scripture still differ on how much of the wording of the songs and speeches is Luke's own; the church has read these chapters as true testimony to what God did, told in the language of the Scriptures that God was fulfilling.

observe: Make two columns for the announcements to Zechariah (verses 5-25) and to Mary (verses 26-38). What elements do they share, and where do they differ?
What does the angel say John will do (verses 15-17), and what does he say Jesus will be (verses 32-35)? What words show that Jesus is greater?
List every Old Testament figure, promise, or phrase you can find echoed in Mary's song and Zechariah's song.
interpret: Zechariah asks “How can I be sure of this?” and Mary asks “How can this be”. Why is one silenced and the other answered?
What does Mary's song mean when it says God has brought down rulers and filled the hungry? Is it describing the past, the present, or the future, and does it make a difference?
Why does Luke open his Gospel with a preface about sources and investigation, and then tell the story in the style of the Old Testament?
apply: Zechariah and Elizabeth were faithful for decades while their deepest prayer went unanswered. How does their story speak to prayers you have been praying for a long time?
Mary asked a real question and then said, “I am the Lord’s servant.” What would it look like for you to bring your honest questions to God and still say yes?
Mary sings that God brings down the proud and lifts up the humble. Where might that song be good news for you, and where might it be a warning?
